findings.title: Last 7 days cost window computed with different semantics in ClaudeSessionScanner/CodexSessionScanner (calendar, up to 8 days) vs OpencodeScanner (rolling 168h)
findings.evidence: ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:50 sevenDaysAgo = startOfToday.addingTimeInterval(-7 * 86400) (same at CodexSessionScanner.swift:94); scan() includes any record with ts >= sevenDaysAgo into totalsLast7 (ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:259-260). Since sevenDaysAgo is midnight 7 days back and now can be up to 23:59 later that same day, the window spans 7-8 calendar days depending on time of day. OpencodeScanner.swift:123 instead computes sevenDaysAgoMs = Int64((now.timeIntervalSince1970 - 7*86400)*1000), an exact rolling 168h cutoff anchored on now, not midnight. For an event exactly 7 days plus 12h before now, Claude/Codex include it in Last 7 days while Opencode excludes the identical elapsed-time event. Same nominal metric, different cutoff rule, computed independently in three files feeding sibling cards in the same UI.
findings.impact: Vendor cards labelled Last 7 days are not apples-to-apples: Claude/Codex systematically include up to about 24h more history than Opencode for the same wall-clock instant, visible on every refresh, not just an edge case.
findings.fix: Extract a single Last7DayWindow.range(now:) helper in AiTaskbarCore consumed by all three scanners, choosing one semantics deliberately (rolling 168h fits the label better), or document the divergence next to the CLAUDE.md cost-scanner table.
findings.cetico_evidence: Same root cause as BUG-ART-006 (ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:50, CodexSessionScanner.swift:94 vs OpencodeScanner.swift:126). Fold it into BUG-ART-006 and do not fix it twice.

findings.title: OpencodeScanner combines tokens with a bare trapping addition before handing off to CostAggregator, bypassing the saturatingAdd invariant built for exactly this hazard
findings.evidence: CostAggregator.swift documents at length why raw Int addition must never be used on vendor-derived token counts (Swift addition TRAPS on overflow; a corrupt input would SIGTRAP the whole menu-bar app) and provides saturatingAdd, used throughout CostAggregator.add and directly in ClaudeSessionScanner.swift:232 and CodexSessionScanner.swift:295. OpencodeScanner.swift:197 builds the ModelUsage passed into CostAggregator.add with outputTokens: max(0, output) plus max(0, reasoning) -- a bare addition on two Int values read straight from sqlite3_column_int64 (lines 185-186), before the safe aggregator ever sees them. Both are clamped at 0 on the low end but unbounded on the high end, so output and reasoning each near Int64.max (a corrupted opencode.db row) trap here, upstream of every saturatingAdd call.
findings.impact: The exact crash scenario saturatingAdd exists to prevent is still reachable through the one scanner that pre-combines two raw columns before calling the shared aggregator. Low likelihood (local db, not network-controlled) but a hard SIGTRAP kills the always-running app with no recovery.
findings.fix: Replace the bare addition with CostAggregator.saturatingAdd(max(0, output), max(0, reasoning)), matching the invariant enforced everywhere else tokens are combined.
findings.cetico_evidence: OpencodeScanner.swift:197 does a bare `max(0, output) + max(0, reasoning)`. SQLite sum() raises on overflow, so each column fits Int64, but two values above 2^62 still make Swift's + trap. The only vector is a corrupted or crafted local opencode.db, which is user-owned, hence LOW.

findings.title: safeSourceURL host/scheme validation duplicated between RSSStatusSource and StatuspageSource with different scheme-recovery behavior
findings.evidence: RSSStatusSource.swift:287-299 and StatuspageSource.swift:352-362 both independently implement a same-host/https-only URL allowlist check (scheme is https, host equals expected host, no user/password/port) building ServiceIncident.sourceURL for the popover UI. RSSStatusSource additionally rewrites a bare host/path string (no scheme) into an https URL before validating (line 290); StatuspageSource has no such rewrite and rejects any string that isn't already a fully-qualified https URL. Both gate the same class of untrusted input (link/shortlink from a remote feed) but were written independently and now enforce different acceptance rules for the identical threat model.
findings.impact: Security-relevant validation logic (host allowlisting for vendor-controlled URLs, the exact class CLAUDE.md's hard rules call out) is duplicated with no cross-reference; a future fix to one implementation has no reason to propagate to the other, so the two status sources can silently drift to different exposure levels for the same incident-link feature.
findings.fix: Extract a single SameOriginURLValidator used by both sources, and decide once whether the bare-host-prefix rewrite belongs in the shared validator or stays an explicit RSS-only pre-step.
findings.cetico_evidence: RSSStatusSource.swift:287-299 and StatuspageSource.swift:352-362 enforce the same security predicate: https scheme, exact host equality with the descriptor host, no user, password or port. RSS's only extra step (L290) prepends https:// to a string that already starts with the expected host, and the result then goes through the same checks, so the acceptance set is no wider. The two copies do not differ in exposure. What remains is about 10 duplicated lines with no defect.

findings.title: AntigravityExecutor lacks the concurrent-drain plus SIGKILL escalation that SecurityToolCredentialReader established for the identical subprocess-hang hazard
findings.evidence: SecurityToolCredentialReader.swift:151-169 explicitly documents and implements draining stdout on a background queue concurrently with waiting for exit (a child that writes more than the pipe buffer can never deadlock against our wait below) and escalates SIGTERM, a 1s grace period, then SIGKILL before giving up. AntigravityExecutor.swift:101-103 reads stdout.fileHandleForReading.readDataToEndOfFile() then stderr's sequentially and synchronously in the same dispatched block that started a 35s timer (lines 83-90) whose handler only calls process.terminate() (SIGTERM, line 88) with no SIGKILL escalation. If agy writes enough to fill either OS pipe buffer before the parent starts reading it, the classic two-pipe deadlock the sibling file's own comment names is directly reproducible here.
findings.impact: A hung or misbehaving agy CLI invocation (network stall, large stderr output, or a process that ignores SIGTERM) can block a background GCD thread indefinitely past the documented 35s budget, on every Gemini/Antigravity refresh cycle -- the exact hazard class the project already paid to characterize and fix once, in the credential reader.
findings.fix: Port the concurrent-drain-then-SIGTERM/SIGKILL-escalation pattern from SecurityToolCredentialReader.runTool into AntigravityExecutor.fetchUsageJSON, or factor both into one shared Process helper in AiTaskbarCore.
findings.cetico_evidence: Duplicate of BP-REP-002 / RACE-CRO-008. SecurityToolCredentialReader.swift:151-168 already drains concurrently and escalates to SIGKILL, but AntigravityExecutor.swift:101-103 does neither. Impact bounded at 35 s.

findings.title: Untrusted Double to Int conversions in ZAIWireTypes/OpenAIWireTypes/GeminiWireTypes bypass the codebase's own safe-conversion pattern (Int(exactly:)), unlike CostAggregator's documented trap-avoidance discipline
findings.evidence: ZAIWireTypes.swift:83-84 does Int($0) on a Double decoded via flexibleDoubleIfPresent, no range check. GeminiWireTypes.swift:154 does Int((rem * 100.0).rounded()) where rem = bucket.remainingFraction is used UNCLAMPED (line 150) even though the sibling consumedFraction two lines above IS clamped to 0...1 before use, in the same function. OpenAIWireTypes.swift:211 and 213 do Int(days.rounded()) / Int(hours.rounded()) on seconds divided by 86400 and 3600, guarded only by seconds greater than 0, no upper bound. Any of these traps (Fatal error: Double value cannot be converted to Int) if the source Double is NaN, infinite, or magnitude at or above 2^63. The codebase already has the right pattern for this hazard: OpenAIResetProtocol.swift:133 uses Int(exactly: count) and returns nil on overflow instead of trapping, and CostAggregator.swift's saturatingAdd doc comment is built on the identical principle for Int arithmetic -- never carried into these three wire-type conversions.
findings.impact: A single out-of-range numeric field in a live ZAI/OpenAI/Gemini API response (server bug, MITM, or future API change) crashes the whole always-running menu-bar app via an uncatchable Swift trap on the next refresh -- more exposed than the local-file scenarios the project already hardened against.
findings.fix: Add a shared safe-int helper (Int(exactly:) after an isFinite check) in AiTaskbarCore/Util and route all wire-type Double to Int conversions through it, mirroring the discipline CostAggregator already documents for Int addition.
findings.cetico_evidence: ZAIWireTypes.swift:82-83 does Int($0) on an unbounded flexibleDoubleIfPresent value. GeminiWireTypes.swift:154 does Int((rem*100).rounded()) with rem unclamped. OpenAIWireTypes.swift:211/213 do Int(days/hours.rounded()) with no upper bound. JSONDecoder rejects NaN and Inf by default, but a finite value such as 1e300 decodes and traps. The vector needs a TLS-authenticated vendor (or the agy CLI output) to send an absurd number, hence LOW.
